cards.text: This psalm's heading says "Of Solomon." Solomon was David's son, and he sat on the throne of his father David (1 Kings 2:12). The whole psalm is a prayer to God for the king, and friend, it does NOT start small.

cards.question: Right out of the gate, the prayer asks God to give the king God's own ___.

cards.text: The prayer asks God to give His righteousness to the son of the king too, and friend, that's one prayer covering TWO royals.

cards.question: With God's justice and righteousness on the list, what does the prayer ask the king to do next?

cards.text: Then the land joins in: "May the mountains bring peace to the people, and the hills bring righteousness." Mountains bringing PEACE, friend, and the only thing my oven ever brings me is the smoke alarm.
Next the prayer asks the king to vindicate the afflicted among the people. Then it turns to the needy and the oppressor.

cards.question: The prayer asks the king to ___ the children of the needy and ___ the oppressor.
The prayer asks for the king to be feared for just one generation.

cards.text: Then the prayer stops sounding like a courtroom and starts sounding like a weather report.

cards.question: The prayer asks for the king to be like rain that falls on freshly cut grass, like spring showers that water the earth. What's that picture about?

answers.text: He brings new life to the land
He brings floods that ruin the land
He stays far above the land

cards.text: The prayer asks for the righteous to flourish in his days and prosperity to abound until the moon is no more. Friend, that's a warranty that outlasts the MOON!

cards.question: So how far does the prayer ask for the king's rule to reach?

answers.text: To the ends of the earth

cards.text: The prayer asks for the nomads to bow before him and his enemies to lick the dust. Friend, I spent YEARS covered in dust in the back of a junk drawer, and I never once licked it.

cards.question: Kings from far-off places show up in the prayer next: the kings of Tarshish and distant shores, and the kings of Sheba and Seba. What does it ask them to bring?

cards.text: Kings from distant shores lining up with gifts, and the farthest anybody ever went for ME was a closing-down sale where I cost a quarter!

cards.question: After those kings from distant shores, the prayer asks for ALL kings to bow down to this king and all nations to serve him.

cards.text: Then comes one little word that changes the feel of the whole prayer: "For." Now we hear what this king will do.

cards.question: After all those kings bowing and gifts coming in, what does the prayer say this king will do?

answers.text: Deliver the needy who cry out
Tax the poor who cry out

cards.question: The prayer says this king only helps the afflicted who already have someone on their side.

cards.text: He will take pity on the poor and needy and save the lives of the oppressed. Kings and gifts are nice, friend, but I think THIS is the part that gets me.

cards.question: The prayer says the king will redeem the oppressed from oppression and violence. Why?

answers.text: Their blood is precious to him

cards.text: Then the prayer cheers out loud: "Long may he live!" It asks for gold from Sheba to be given him, and friend, every king needs a hype man like this in his corner.

cards.question: The prayer asks people to ___ for the king and ___ him all day long.

cards.text: Then it asks for an abundance of grain swaying atop the hills, and fruit trees flourishing like the forests of Lebanon. Grain growing on HILLTOPS, friend, and I can't get one batch to bake even on a flat pan.

cards.question: The prayer pictures the people of the land's cities too. What does it say they'll be like?

cards.text: The prayer asks for the king's name to endure forever, as long as the sun shines. My name's carved into my handle, and THAT'S as forever as I get.

cards.question: The prayer asks for all nations to be blessed in this king.

cards.text: Then the prayer lifts its eyes from the king to the LORD God, the God of Israel, and blesses Him.

cards.question: The prayer says the king does marvelous deeds right alongside the LORD.
Blessing God's glorious name forever, the prayer asks for all the earth to be filled with the LORD's ___.

cards.text: The praise closes with "Amen and amen." One amen means you agree, friend, but two means you're signing it in front of witnesses.

cards.question: One more line sits at the very end of the psalm, after the amens. What does it say concludes here?

answers.text: The prayers of David son of Jesse
The songs of Solomon son of David
The words of Moses son of Amram

findings.problem: The card says the whole psalm is a prayer for the king. Verses 18-19 bless the LORD God, not the king, and verse 20 is a closing note about David's prayers. The card also cites only Psalm 72:1 while making a claim about the whole psalm.

rule.text: Noticing: What he points out must be true.

findings.problem: "One prayer covering TWO royals" decides that "the king" and "the son of the king" in verse 1 are two different people. The text doesn't say whether they are two people or one king described twice, so this should stay open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The question says the prayer asks the king to judge God's people. Verse 2 is "May he judge," said to God about the king, so the prayer is not speaking to the king. The same wording appears on stop 1 card 6 ("asks the king to vindicate") and stop 1 card 7 ("asks the king to ___").

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: This story card is a bare summary with none of Papa Dorin's voice. It reads like a study note, not like the storyteller.

rule.text: Short, but not stripped down. A story card still has enough of Papa Dorin's voice and enough context that the moment makes sense.

findings.problem: This story card only repeats verse 10, which card 14 already covered, and adds a joke. It tells nothing new from the passage and does not move the baker forward.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage.

findings.problem: "The prayer asks people to ___ for the king" turns the text's wish ("May people ever pray for him; may they bless him") into a direct request to people.

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: The setup inside the question, "Blessing God's glorious name," gives away the blank's answer, "glory."

rule.text: No card ever gives away the answer to a choice card that comes later.

findings.problem: The psalm is headed "Of Solomon" but ends with "Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse." Without any context, this may confuse the baker. The closing line is generally understood as the end of a collection of psalms.
findings.question: Should Prep add an outside fact that explains a closing note like Psalm 72:20, or leave the line unexplained? The docs allow outside facts "when they help" but never say when they are needed for the baker to understand the passage.
